Implementing a CNN in FPGA Programmable

Logic for NILM Applications

Abstract—Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) techniques are gaining popularity in the field of energy savings. Generally implemented through the use of smart meters, the main challenge with these devices is that they operate at very low sampling rates. To address this issue, FPGA-based systems have been proposed to capture instantaneous currents and voltages at higher sampling frequencies in the kHz range. However, the limitation of these architectures lies in the fact that the acquired windows are often transmitted upstream to the cloud for the application of load classification algorithms based on machine learning, relying on high-bandwidth communications available onsite. This work proposes an alternative approach by implementing the classification algorithms in the same acquisition and processing system, by using custom convolutional neural networks on mid-range FPGA devices. Brevitas and FINN frameworks are used for the quantization-aware training, as well as for the generation of a peripheral that may be integrated into any FPGA-based SoC (System-on-Chip) architecture. The proposed approach allows the whole processing involved in NILM techniques to be integrated into a single embedded system. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Keywords—Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM), Systemon-Chip (SoC), Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN)

The increase in energy consumption is becoming a major challenge nowadays. Energy disaggregation techniques have gained popularity in the field of energy savings and are expected to be able to significantly reduce consumption in both residential and commercial environments with advances in Smart Meters and classification algorithms [1].

Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) techniques are energy disaggregation techniques that propose to identify the loads connected to the grid through the energy consumption in the mains [2], usually obtained by the use of smart meters. The main problem with these commercial devices is that they usually work at very low sampling rates (around 1 Hz), so the number of extractable features is much lower than working at higher sampling frequencies, in the range of kHz [3]. The drawback of increasing the sampling rate is the sheer amount of data to deal with. To solve this, solutions based on event detectors are often used. In [4, 5] FPGA-based (Field- Programmable Gate Array) SoC (Systems-on-Chip) architectures oriented to the implementation of real-time NILM techniques are proposed. These architectures integrate Analog Front-Ends (AFE) for capturing instantaneous

currents and voltages at sampling rates up to 4 kHz, to subsequently implement an event detection phase that allows capturing configurable size windows around the events for their identification. The limitation of these architectures lies in the fact that the acquired windows are transmitted upstream to the cloud for the application of intelligent algorithms for load classification. Therefore, these systems rely on highbandwidth communications to send high-frequency current and voltage waveforms.

An alternative may be to compute locally the classification methods by implementing them in the same acquisition and processing system. Within classification algorithms, using artificial neural networks (ANN) is widespread [6]; specifically, convolutional neural networks (CNN) are a type of ANN widely used in computer vision and image classification. In [7] a CNN architecture is proposed for the identification of loads in the NILM environment, through the generation of images from the temporal windows of the electric current. These temporal windows correspond to the events produced in the electrical network and captured at high frequency by systems such as those proposed in [4, 5].

Considering the acquisition and processing stages, FPGA devices are a feasible option for the implementation of NILM techniques, as they are able to handle the computational load in real time, with sampling rates in the kHz range due to their parallelization capability. As for the classification stage, the implementation of CNN on FPGA devices has already been extensively studied over the last few years [8-11]. Although these types of algorithms have typically been implemented on GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) due to their high performance over general-purpose processors, it is well known that FPGAs are more efficient in terms of power consumption. In addition to the above, improvements in both FPGA device technology and the ability of FPGAs to handle both parallelism and compact data types (e.g., binary operations) benefit them over GPUs [12].

When it comes to implementing CNN on FPGA devices, there are different ways to approach it, from coding the network directly in HDL (Hardware Definition Language) [13] to using tools for working in high-level languages, such as those offered by Vitis HLS tools [14]. As neural networks have gained popularity in the hardware environment, different frameworks have emerged to ease or simplify the implementation process. Some examples are the popular HLS4ML [15] or F-CNN [16], the former being an environment focused on the post-training implementation, whereas the latter is focused on the training process. Vitis AI [17] is a Xilinx's development platform for AI inference on its own devices through the use of its DPU cores, dedicated engines for convolutional neural networks but only available on certain devices. The FINN project [18-20], a framework from Xilinx Research Labs, focuses on the inference of binary

Although it has already been demonstrated that neural networks with binary quantifications can achieve accurate classification [21, 22], FINN framework allows working with different bit-width quantization for weights and activations, adapting them to the accuracy and resource consumption needs of the target application. Among its tools, FINN includes Brevitas [23], a Pytorch library for the implementation and training of quantized neural networks.

This work presents an analysis for the implementation of custom convolutional neural networks on mid-range FPGA devices, where memory resources are limited. Using Brevitas, the initial neural network is quantized and adapted for further implementation on an FPGA device. Instead of proceeding with quantization after training the network, Brevitas enables quantization-aware training, reducing the impact of quantization on the CNN performance. After the neural network has been quantized and trained, the FINN framework is used to generate a peripheral that may be integrated into any FPGA-based SoC architecture through Xilinx development tools. Based on previously customized neural networks for NILM techniques developed in [7], the main novelty of the proposal is the possibility of integrating the whole processing involved in NILM techniques in a single embedded system, from signal acquisition and event detection to the classification of loads connected to the mains. The rest of the manuscript is organized as follows: Section II describes a general overview of the proposed study and its possible applications; Section III deals with the implementation process of a neural network carried out on a FPGA device; Section IV presents some experimental results; and, finally, some conclusions are discussed in Section V.

In [7] three ANN architectures for load identification are proposed and presented, with different levels of complexity and number of parameters. All the proposals correspond to convolutional neural networks, divided into a feature extraction stage followed by a feature classification stage to identify the different loads connected to the power grid.

Since convolutional neural networks work mainly by image classification, the proposal presents a preprocessing stage, where temporal windows are created around the events (on/off) of the electrical appliances, with a window length of 4096 samples, obtained from the electric current. Electric current samples at 4kHz shows changes both in amplitude and in its spectral components, thus allowing the classification stage to be able to identify the corresponding load. In order to get the images ready for the classification stage, they are built by successive rows of 64 samples coming from the aforementioned current window, thus obtaining an image of 64×64 samples. Fig. 1 shows an example of an image obtained from an event caused by the connection of a household appliance, in this case, a printer.

Since the objective of this proposal is the implementation of a CNN on a SoC using its programmable logic, the second architecture presented in [7] has been selected a reference design, since it presents a significantly lower number of parameters than the alternatives with similar results. Additionally, in order to proceed with its implementation, a quantification process has been carried out to reduce the size and computational load of the network, as well as minor

modifications to adapt and facilitate the workflow of the implementation tools used.
Fig. 1. Example of generated image from captured electric current used for load classification in [7], for 4096 long windows (64x64 images).

The data used to train and validate the implemented neural network were obtained from the BLUED [24] database. This database contains information on the current and voltage consumptions of a house over 8 days; this information has been sampled at 12 kHz, although, in order to reduce the amount of information to be processed, it was reduced to 4 kHz. The database also contains information on both the timestamp at which the events occurred and the appliance that caused them, facilitating the process of labeling the images for the training of the CNN. The dataset has been divided into three groups: training, validation, and test.

On the other hand, the main purpose of the implementation of the aforementioned CNN on an FPGA device is the possibility of integrating it as part of an embedded system whose objective is the application of NILM techniques. In [4, 5] a SoC architecture based on Xilinx Zynq- 7000 is proposed, oriented to the real-time implementation of NILM techniques as an alternative to the use of Smart Meters. This proposal uses an ADE9153A integrated circuit as analog front-end (AFE) for capturing both instantaneous current and voltage at the input of the household, allowing to sample both signals at high frequency (in the range of a few kHz). The whole system implements different peripherals for both the management of the acquired signals and their processing. The main novelty of the proposal is the implementation of a configurable system that allows the detection of the on/offswitching events for the different loads connected to the mains by analyzing the captured windows. A schematic of the whole system is shown in Fig. 2.

Although, in both architectures, the windows of the different events occurring in the electrical network are captured, they are transmitted to the cloud through different protocols for their subsequent classification. By integrating the peripheral developed in this work, an embedded system that implements all stages of NILM techniques is possible, from the detection and capture of events to their load classification, all in a single local architecture.
Fig. 2. General block diagram of the developed SoC architecture in [4, 5], together with the proposed CNN implementation integration.

For the implementation of the CNN in an FPGA device, a framework developed by Xilinx Research Labs called FINN has been used. The purpose of this framework is to generate a specific workflow for each type of network, resulting in a specific implementation directly on the programmable logic of the SoC, focusing especially on the implementation of quantized neural networks. Although FINN is oriented to the generation of drivers for use in PYNQ devices, it also allows the generation of peripherals defined in Verilog, allowing them to be implemented on any FPGA device with enough logic and memory space to do so.

In addition, to carrying out a specific implementation for each neural network, one of the main advantages of FINN is the versatility and manipulation that it allows during the implementation process. During the workflow, FINN enables the configuration of different parameters in the network, such as: the storage method, either in RAM or directly in logic; their access (allowing to access and modify the value of the weights at runtime); and its size or bit width. It also allows to carry out all these modifications individually for each one of the layers that build the network. This offers versatility and adaptation to the FPGA where a specific neural network is intended to be implemented, dealing with limited logic and memory resources. Fig. 3 shows the workflow to be followed when working with this framework.

Nevertheless, FINN offers in its libraries different standardized databases and quantified and pre-trained networks for its implementation. It also allows working with external data and networks developed by third parties. For this purpose, the starting point is a neural network previously implemented in Pytorch and a dataset for the training and validation phases, which were previously presented in Section II. Since FINN works with quantized neural networks, the framework provides Brevitas, which is a Pytorch library for neural network quantization. One of the main advantages offered by Brevitas is the quantization-aware training, which allows obtaining better results in terms of model accuracy compared to post-training quantization. Due to some limitations of FINN implementation process with certain neural network configurations, the CNN presented above has been slightly modified, as shown in Fig. 4, and detailed in Table 1. Once the network has been quantified and trained until the desired results are obtained, its parameters can be exported to FINN to start with the peripheral generation.
Fig. 3. FINN workflow for ANN implementation on FPGA devices using peripheral generation.

As described in Fig. 3, the FINN workflow starts from a quantized network trained in Brevitas until finally obtaining the peripheral. During the process, a series of transformations are performed to eliminate floating-point operations and reach a model composed of different modules belonging to the FINN libraries. These resulting modules can be converted into HLS language and, therefore, implemented in an FPGA.

At this point in the process, FINN allows to configure, on one side, how the parameters from each layer are stored and accessed, as well as their level of parallelization, resulting in a trade-off between the resource consumption and the latency of the model. Therefore, it is possible to adapt the artificial neural networks to work in FPGA devices with limited logic and memory resources. Once the necessary configurations have been made to obtain both the desired consumption and latency, the result is a peripheral composed itself by different modules developed in HLS, where each module corresponds to the layers of the neural network and the nodes resulting from the transformations performed by FINN, connected to each other with FIFO memories. The peripheral has been previously synthesized for the FPGA selected by the FINN tools through calls to Vivado and Vitis HLS tools and can be implemented.

The generated peripheral, which integrates the optimized CNN for NILM techniques, has been implemented on the Zybo z7-20 board, a Zynq-7000 SoC [25] which is a device from Xilinx, Inc., which has both an ARM processor and a programmable logic in its architecture. This is a mid-range SoC with limited logic and memory resources, where it is possible to leverage FINN's ability to manipulate resource consumption individually for each layer composing the neural network.

As shown in Table I, the bit width for the weights in all layers has been reduced to 3 bits to maintain a balance between consumption and performance, except for the first dense layer of the classification stage, which has been reduced to 2 bits due to its high number of parameters. Although FINN

Since in NILM applications latency is not a determining factor (usually not more than a few frames per second), the latency has been reduced in order to minimize resource consumption. The estimated latency for the design is 21 frames per second with a 100 MHz clock, more than enough for this type of applications. FINN also offers the possibility of enabling or eliminating the use of DSPs for each layer, reducing the consumption of other resources, and of storing them in RAM and in logical memory (LUTRAM), all this by means of a JSON file. As mentioned above, the layer that concentrates most of the network resources is the first dense layer in the classification stage, so its parameters have been stored in RAM memory while the other layers, having a smaller number of parameters, have been stored in logical memory.

Once the peripheral (IP) corresponding to the neural network has been generated with the aforementioned configurations, in order to test it, a SoC architecture has been implemented in Vivado that has both the developed IP and an ARM core, whereas a DMA peripheral will be in charge of moving the test image samples (preloaded in DDR memory) directly to the network IP and reading the resulting load classification. In addition, the ground-truth classification data of the test images have also been loaded into memory, in order to evaluate the results and compare them with those obtained prior to the implementation in the FPGA device. It is worth noting that, to make use of the DMA on the generated IP, it is necessary to add an extra transformation to the standard FINN workflow to enable the TLAST signal, used by this communication protocol.

Finally, Fig. 5 and Table III show the resulting confusion matrices and performance metrics of the original neural network (CNN), after the quantization process (QCNN) and implementing the neural network directly on the FPGA device (QCNN FPGA), using the whole set of test images. Considering both the quantification process and the reduction in the bit width for the weights from the different layers, as well as the implementation directly on the programmable logic, the metrics that assess the performance of a neural network have been reduced by just 1~2 % with respect to its original performance, remaining above 95 % in all cases. Note that some classes may be more affected by the quantification process, such class 00 in Fig. 5. Although the network has been optimized to take full advantage of the resources of the target FPGA, especially in terms of memory, these can be adjusted depending on the final system requirements.

This work presents an example of a convolutional neural network implementation in FPGA devices, including its integration in a SoC architecture. The studied CNN is proposed for NILM techniques, where it processes the electrical current acquired around an on-off switching from an appliance. This algorithm is capable of classifying the load responsible for the on/off event. Brevitas and FINN frameworks have been used for the quantization-aware training, as well as for the generation of the peripheral resulting from the quantized CNN. The followed procedure allows to significantly reduce the resource consumption by limiting the width of the network parameters and increasing the system parallelization. Due to this reduction in word width and the quantification process, the obtained results show a reduction of only 1~2 % in the metrics that assess the performance of the neural network with respect to its original floating-point version, making the system suitable for integration into a SoC architecture.
